inline.s: [The mind dwelling in dharmas] Clinging to the mark of dharmas, harboring the mind that there are realms, merits, and fruit-stages to be obtained. [Darkness] Same as “gloom.”

Cultivation is detachment from marks; if the mind dwells in dharmas, that is clinging to marks, and one goes south while driving north. It is like rowing a boat across a lake on a pitch-black night, wanting to reach the far shore: on and on one rows, and the bow has already turned away from the destination without one even knowing it. Giving while dwelling in dharmas may win the praise of others, and one may feel quite good about it; but if love and hate, grasping and rejecting, greed, anger, delusion, and pride—this root of birth and death—do not decrease but increase, then one has entered a wrong path and will surely stir up a host of demonic obstructions: seeking to rise, one falls instead. Moreover, giving while clinging to marks is merit-with-outflows rather than virtue, and though one may enjoy blessings in the next life because of it, by doing evil in reliance on those blessings, in the life after that one falls into evil paths. Hence the Song of Certifying the Way says: “Giving while clinging to marks brings heavenly blessings, like shooting an arrow straight into the sky; when its force is spent, the arrow falls back down, bringing a next life full of disappointment.”

The “dharmas” here, as in the preceding sentence, also mean the dharma of the Way, that is, the theory, method, realm, and fruit-stage of cultivating the Way. The passage above said not to give while dwelling in form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; here it says one should also not give while dwelling in the mark of dharmas (merit-with-outflows, virtue, fruit-stage). Giving is not to inflate the self but to dissolve the self.
If the bodhisattva's mind does not dwell in dharmas and so practices giving, it is like a man with eyes, illumined by the light of the sun, seeing all the various colors”

—if the bodhisattva's mind does not dwell in dharmas and so practices giving, it is like a man with eyes whose light of wisdom shines brightly, so that the direction and the road are seen perfectly clearly.

[The mind does not dwell in dharmas and so practices giving] To practice giving without seeking and without clinging (the three wheels are empty). “The mind does not dwell in dharmas” is not clinging to the mark of dharmas. [Seeing all the various colors] The “colors” here are the dust of form, meaning all visible realms and objects.

Subhuti! In future ages, if good men and good women can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the Tathāgata, by Buddha-wisdom, will know such people fully and see such people fully, and they will all accomplish immeasurable and boundless merit.

Above it was said that the dharma the Tathāgata obtained within this great dream is also illusion. That being so, the bodhisattva's mind should not dwell in the mark of dharmas. But the World-Honored One feared that deluded people might thereby fall into the view of annihilation and dwell in the mark of non-dharmas, and so he added with care: “Subhuti! In future ages, if good men and good women can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the Tathāgata, by Buddha-wisdom, will know such people fully and see such people fully, and they will all accomplish immeasurable and boundless merit.”

blocks.text: Chapter Fifteen: The Merit of Upholding the Sutra

inline.s: The World-Honored One teaches that this sutra has inconceivable, immeasurable, boundless merit.

Subhuti! If good men and good women give in charity their bodies as many times as the sands of the Ganges in the first portion of the day, and again in the middle portion of the day give in charity their bodies as many times as the sands of the Ganges, and in the latter portion of the day also give in charity their bodies as many times as the sands of the Ganges, thus giving their bodies for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas; and if again someone hears this sutra and has faith without opposition, that person's merit surpasses the former—how much more so one who writes it out, receives, upholds, reads, and recites it, and explains it for others.

Subhuti! If good men and good women give in charity their bodies and lives as many times as the sands of the Ganges in the morning, and again at noon give in charity their bodies and lives as many times as the sands of the Ganges, and in the evening again give in charity their bodies and lives as many times as the sands of the Ganges, thus three times a day giving their bodies and lives as many times as the sands of the Ganges for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas; and if another person hears this sutra and has faith without opposition, the merit he obtains surpasses the former—how much more so if he also writes out the Diamond Sutra, receives, upholds, reads, and recites it, and explains it for others: the merit he obtains surpasses the former by a number beyond reckoning!

[First portion of the day] Ancient India divided a day and night into six portions, each portion equal to four hours today. The daytime portions are the first portion of the day, the middle portion of the day, and the latter portion of the day; the nighttime portions are the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch. [Kalpa] The extremely long time through which a world passes in formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness is called a kalpa.

Subhuti! In brief, this sutra has inconceivable, immeasurable, boundless merit. The Tathāgata speaks it for those who have aroused the Mahāyāna mind, and speaks it for those who have aroused the supreme vehicle mind.

Subhuti! In brief, this sutra has inconceivable, immeasurable, boundless merit. This is what the Tathāgata speaks for those who have aroused the mind to receive and uphold the Mahāyāna Buddhadharma, and for those who have aroused the mind to receive and uphold the supreme vehicle Buddhadharma.
Here the World-Honored One clearly points out the ones for whom this sutra is intended.

[Mahāyāna] The bodhisattva's dharma-gate, whose aim is to save the world and benefit others, and whose highest fruit is the Buddha-fruit. The Mahāyāna, from an ordinary being's cultivation to Buddhahood, must pass through fifty-two stages: the ten stages of faith, the ten stages of abiding, the ten stages of practice, the ten stages of dedication, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment. [Supreme vehicle] The highest and unsurpassed teaching, that is, the perfect and sudden teaching, also called the One Buddha Vehicle or the One Vehicle. [Speaks it for those who have aroused the supreme vehicle mind] Speaks it for those who have aroused the mind to receive and uphold the supreme vehicle Buddhadharma.

If someone can receive, uphold, read, and recite it and widely explain it for others, the Tathāgata knows such people fully and sees such people fully, and they all accomplish immeasurable, inexpressible, boundless, inconceivable merit. Such people bear the Tathāgata's anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

If someone can receive, uphold, read, and recite it and widely explain it for others, the Tathāgata knows these people fully and foresees these people fully, and they all accomplish immeasurable, inexpressible, boundless, inconceivable merit. Such people are taking up the family inheritance of the Tathāgata's “unsurpassed perfect enlightenment”; they are the Buddha's dharma-heirs.

This sutra is the road to Buddhahood; the cultivator who walks along the road has true benefit and inconceivable merit. The point on which receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting come to rest is this: deeply believing without doubt, and practicing as taught.

Why? Subhuti! Those who delight in the small dharma, clinging to the view of a self, the view of a human, the view of a being, and the view of a life, cannot hear, accept, read, or recite this sutra, nor explain it for others.

Why is it that “such people bear the Tathāgata's anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi”? Because those who delight in the small vehicle's Buddhadharma cling to the view of a self, the view of a human, the view of a being, and the view of a life, and so toward this sutra (the Diamond Sutra) they cannot hear, accept, read, or recite it, nor explain it for others; they cannot take up the family inheritance of the Tathāgata's “unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.”
From this we know that not clinging to the view of a self, the view of a human, the view of a being, and the view of a life is the key to receiving and upholding the Diamond Sutra.

[Small dharma] The dharma of the small vehicle. The Lotus Sutra says: “Those of dull faculties delight in the small dharma.” “People of dull faculties and small wisdom, who cling to marks and are proud and arrogant, cannot believe this dharma.” (“This dharma” means the One Vehicle Buddhadharma.) [View of a life] That is, the view of a life span. The Buddha Treasury Sutra says: “The Buddha, having attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, does not teach the dharma for people of wrong views and evil ways, nor for those who hold the view of a self, the view of a human, the view of a being, and the view of a life span.” [View of a self] Falsely clinging to the body and mind of the five aggregates as a self. [View of a human] Falsely clinging to the body and mind of the five aggregates of others as another. [View of a being] Falsely clinging to the body and mind of the five aggregates of beings as beings. [View of a life] Falsely clinging to the life span of the form body as one's own life span.

The Complete Enlightenment Sutra says: “What is ignorance? Good man! All beings, from beginningless time, have various inversions, like a deluded person who mistakes the four directions for one another, falsely taking the four great elements as the mark of their own body and the conditioned shadows of the six dusts as the mark of their own mind. It is like a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good man! In the sky there truly are no flowers; the diseased one falsely clings to them, and because of this false clinging he is not only deluded about the self-nature of this emptiness but also deluded about where the real flowers arise. From this false existence he turns through birth and death; therefore it is called ignorance.” [The conditioned shadows of the six dusts] The images that arise in dependence on the six dusts, that is, the thoughts that arise when the six faculties meet the six dusts.

Subhuti! Wherever this sutra may be, all the heavenly beings, humans, and asuras of every world should make offerings to it. You should know that such a place is a stupa. All should revere it, bow, and circumambulate it, and scatter flowers and incense there.

Subhuti! Wherever this sutra may be, all the heavenly beings, humans, and asuras of every world should come to make offerings. You should know that such a place (where the Diamond Sutra is) is a stupa and temple of the Buddha. All should revere it, bow, and walk in circumambulation, and scatter various flowers and incense around it.

[Bowing and circumambulating] Bowing and walking in circumambulation (to the right). [Flowers and incense] Flowers and incense. “Flowers” is the same as blossoms, representing the cultivation of the cause; incense represents the true incense of precepts, concentration, and wisdom. There are rubbed incense, powdered incense, and pellet incense, and so on. “Pellet incense” is made by mixing various incenses into pellets. [The true incense of precepts, concentration, and wisdom] When one's own mind has no wrong, no evil, no jealousy, no greed or anger, no robbery or harm—this is called the incense of precepts. When one sees all good and evil conditions and marks and one's own mind is not disturbed—this is called the incense of concentration. When one's own mind is without obstruction, constantly contemplates the self-nature with wisdom, does not create any evil, and though cultivating all good, does not cling in mind; honoring those above and remembering those below, and taking pity on and succoring the orphaned and poor—this is called the incense of wisdom.
The World-Honored One teaches the immense power of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra: purifying karmic obstructions and realizing the sage-fruit.

Furthermore, Subhuti! If good men and good women receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra and are despised by others, this is because of evil karma from former lives that should have led them to fall into evil paths. Because in this present life they are despised by others, their evil karma from former lives is thereby extinguished, and they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Not only that, Subhuti! If good men and good women receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra and are despised by others, this is because the evil karma created in the past (including this life before receiving and reciting this sutra, and in former lives) would by rights have led them, after death, to fall at once into evil paths. Now, because they receive, uphold, read, and recite the Diamond Sutra, though in this life they are despised by others, the evil karma created in the past is thereby extinguished, and they shall realize the Buddha-fruit.

This teaches that receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra turns heavy karma into light retribution: the heavy karma is falling into evil paths after death, and the light retribution is being despised by others in this life; and the merit obtained is immense:
they shall realize the Buddha-fruit
[They shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi] They shall realize the Buddha-fruit.

On the bodhi path, obstructions caused by past evil karma are everywhere, and so it is of the utmost importance for cultivators to repent of karmic obstructions. Yet some karma admits of repentance and some does not. If the offense is extremely heavy and has become fixed karma, repentance is especially difficult. In the scripture, “evil paths” shows that this is heavy karma, and “should have led them to fall” shows that it is fixed karma. Good men and good women who have heavy karma that has become fixed karma, now receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting this sutra, are merely despised by others (heavy karma turned into light retribution, fixed karma already transformed), and they will certainly realize the Buddha-fruit. This teaches the immense power of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra: purifying karmic obstructions and realizing the sage-fruit.
From this passage we can also see that those for whom the Diamond Sutra is intended further include good men and good women who, because of evil karma from former lives, should fall into evil paths.

For whom, after all, was the Diamond Sutra spoken? This is an extremely important question. In “Chapter Two, on Good Manifestation's Request,” we see that this sutra was spoken by the World-Honored One in response to the Elder Subhuti's request, for good men and good women who have just aroused the great mind. Moreover, in “Chapter Six, on Right Faith and Rarity,” it says: “After the Tathāgata's extinction, in the last five hundred years, there will be those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit; toward these chapters and verses they can give rise to faith, taking them as true.” In “Chapter Fifteen, on the Merit of Upholding the Sutra,” it says: this is what the Tathāgata speaks for those who have aroused the mind to study the Mahāyāna, and speaks for those who have aroused the mind to study the supreme vehicle. (Scripture: “The Tathāgata speaks it for those who have aroused the Mahāyāna mind, and speaks it for those who have aroused the supreme vehicle mind.”) Here the World-Honored One also says: good men and good women who, because of past evil karma, should fall into evil paths, can also receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, “and because in this present life they are despised by others, their evil karma from former lives is thereby extinguished, and they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.” Therefore we know that the Diamond Sutra is spoken for good men and good women who have just aroused the great mind and for beings above them. The basic condition for receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra is this: keeping the precepts and cultivating merit. Even those good men and good women who, because of past evil karma, should fall into evil paths can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, and thereby realize the Buddha-fruit.

Subhuti! I recall that in past ages, countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, before Dipankara Buddha, I met eight hundred forty million billion nayuta Buddhas, and served and made offerings to them all, without passing by a single one. If again someone, in a later age of decline, can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit he obtains—compared with the merit of my offerings to all those Buddhas—mine does not come to one hundredth of his, nor to one thousand ten-thousand millionth of his, indeed not to any fraction expressible by reckoning or simile.

Subhuti! Thinking back over countless kalpas past, before I met Dipankara Buddha I encountered eight hundred forty million billion nayuta Buddhas, and I made offerings to and served them all, without passing by a single one. If someone in a later age of decline can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, then the merit he obtains—compared with the merit of my offerings to all those Buddhas—my merit does not come to one hundredth of his, nor to one thousand ten-thousand millionth of his, indeed not to any fraction of the immense number that reckoning and simile cannot describe.
[Asaṃkhyeya] Rendered in Chinese as “countless,” meaning so many that no number can calculate them. [Nayuta] A numeral, equal to the hundred million of today.

This passage shows that the merit of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting this sutra exceeds the merit of making offerings to Buddhas by far, far more. This tells us that even the merit of making offerings to Buddhas is hard to compare with the merit of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting this sutra, how much less other merits.

Subhuti! If good men and good women, in a later age of decline, receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, and I were to set forth fully the merit they obtain, some who heard it would become mad and confused in mind, doubting and disbelieving. Subhuti! You should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its karmic reward is also inconceivable.

The World-Honored One said to Subhuti: Subhuti! If good men and good women, in the future age of the Dharma's decline, receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, and I were to set forth fully the merit they obtain, some who heard it would become deranged and confused in mind, doubting and disbelieving, and even give rise to slander and so create great evil karma; and so I truly have not yet set forth fully the merit of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra! Subhuti! You should know that the grandeur and depth of the meaning of this sutra cannot be imagined by the mind, nor expressed or discussed in words, and that the immensity of the karmic reward of receiving and upholding this sutra likewise cannot be imagined by the mind, nor expressed or discussed in words.

[If I were to set forth fully] If I were to set forth all of it. [Doubting fox] Extremely doubtful. The fox is by nature full of doubt, and so the fox is used as a simile. [Inconceivable] That which cannot be thought or imagined by the mind, nor expressed or discussed in words.

Above, the World-Honored One said that he had not yet set forth fully the merit of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra! Then how much merit and blessing has the World-Honored One set forth in the Diamond Sutra? The World-Honored One explains by similes:
1. Compared with giving the seven treasures

Subhuti! What do you think: if a person filled a three-thousand-great-thousand world with the seven treasures and gave them away, . . . and if again someone, within this sutra, receives and upholds even a four-line verse and expounds it for others, his merit surpasses the former.”
(Chapter Eight, on the Birth of All in Accord with the Dharma)

“Subhuti! Suppose all the grains of sand in the Ganges River, and as many Ganges Rivers as those grains of sand: what do you think, are the grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers not many? Subhuti said: Very many, World-Honored One! Even the Ganges Rivers alone are countless in number, how much more their grains of sand. Subhuti! I now tell you in truth. If there were good men and good women who filled with the seven treasures as many three-thousand-great-thousand worlds as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers, and gave them away, would the merit they obtain be great? Subhuti said: Very great, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Subhuti: If good men and good women, within this sutra, receive and uphold even a four-line verse and expound it for others, this merit surpasses the former merit.”
(Chapter Eleven, on the Merit of the Unconditioned Being Supreme)

“Subhuti! If in a three-thousand-great-thousand world, a person took all the kings of Mount Sumeru and heaps of seven treasures such as these and gave them away; and if a person received, upheld, read, and recited even a four-line verse of this Prajñā-Pāramitā Sutra and expounded it for others, the former merit does not come to one hundredth of this, nor to one hundred thousand ten-thousand millionth of this, indeed not to any fraction expressible by reckoning or simile.”
(Chapter Twenty-four, on Merit and Wisdom Being Beyond Compare)

“Subhuti! If a person filled measureless asaṃkhyeya worlds with the seven treasures and gave them away; and if good men and good women who have aroused the bodhi mind held to this sutra, even a four-line verse, received, upheld, read, and recited it, and expounded it for others, their merit surpasses the former.”
(Chapter Thirty-two, on Response-Bodies Being Not True)
2. Compared with making offerings to Buddhas

“Subhuti! I recall that in past ages, countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, before Dipankara Buddha, I met eight hundred forty million billion nayuta Buddhas, and served and made offerings to them all, without passing by a single one; if again someone, in a later age of decline, can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit he obtains—compared with the merit of my offerings to all those Buddhas—does not come to one hundredth of his, nor to one thousand ten-thousand millionth of his, indeed not to any fraction expressible by reckoning or simile.”
(Chapter Sixteen, on Purifying Karmic Obstructions)
3. Compared with giving one's body and life

“Subhuti! If good men and good women give in charity their bodies and lives as many times as the sands of the Ganges; and if again someone, within this sutra, receives and upholds even a four-line verse and expounds it for others, the latter's merit is far greater.”
(Chapter Thirteen, on Receiving and Upholding in Accord with the Dharma)

“Subhuti! If good men and good women give in charity their bodies as many times as the sands of the Ganges in the first portion of the day, and again in the middle portion of the day give in charity their bodies as many times as the sands of the Ganges, and in the latter portion of the day also give in charity their bodies as many times as the sands of the Ganges, thus giving their bodies for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas; and if again someone hears this sutra and has faith without opposition, that person's merit surpasses the former—how much more so one who writes it out, receives, upholds, reads, and recites it, and explains it for others.”
(Chapter Fifteen, on the Merit of Upholding the Sutra)
Not only that: the Diamond Sutra can also extinguish karmic obstructions. In this section the World-Honored One says:

“If good men and good women receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra and are despised by others, this is because of evil karma from former lives that should have led them to fall into evil paths. Because in this present life they are despised by others, their evil karma from former lives is thereby extinguished, and they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

This says: receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra can extinguish even karma that should lead to the evil paths, and one shall realize the Buddha-fruit; then the lighter karma that obstructs our practice and our daily life can certainly be extinguished as well. The power and benefit of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra are truly immense beyond words!

Therefore, to receive, uphold, read, and recite the Diamond Sutra and expound it for others is not only to cultivate wisdom but also to cultivate merit and extinguish karmic obstructions—it is the double cultivation of merit and wisdom!
The first half of this sutra ends here.
The second half of this sutra begins with this section.

No-self is the center of this sutra: breaking the two selves—the self of persons (clinging to a self) and the self of dharmas (clinging to dharmas). The first half of this sutra breaks the self of persons, and the second half breaks the self of dharmas. The scripture of this section says: “in truth there is no dharma by which one arouses the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,” “in truth there is no dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,” “in truth there is no dharma called a bodhisattva”; hence this section is titled “Ultimate No-Self.”
Then Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! Good men and good women who arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—how should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?

At that time Subhuti again respectfully asked the Buddha: World-Honored One! Good men and good women who have aroused the great mind of becoming a Buddha and liberating beings—how should they abide and uphold it? How should they subdue their minds?

By the end of the preceding chapter, the questions seem already to have been answered, the sutra's name and the merit of receiving, upholding, and transmitting it have been given, and generally speaking the scripture should end here. But what the World-Honored One teaches is the great dharma of becoming a Buddha, of the utmost importance; and though the Elder Subhuti deeply understood its meaning and purport (Chapter Fourteen: “Then, when Subhuti had heard this sutra expounded, he understood its meaning and purport deeply, and with tears of grief and joy he wept.”) and could believe, understand, receive, and uphold it (Chapter Fourteen: “World-Honored One! I now hear such a sutra, and to believe, understand, receive, and uphold it is not difficult”), yet considering that this teaching's meaning and purport are profound and wondrous (in Chapter Fourteen Subhuti said to the Buddha: “Rare indeed, World-Honored One! The Buddha has expounded a sutra so profoundly deep. From of old, though I have obtained the wisdom-eye, I had never heard such a sutra”), he hoped the World-Honored One would further clarify: how, through this sutra, does one ultimately reach the other shore? And so he again asked the same questions (how should they abide? how should they subdue their minds?), requesting the World-Honored One's teaching.

The Buddha told Subhuti: Good men and good women who arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should thus give rise to the mind: I should liberate all beings, and when all beings have been liberated, not one being has in fact been liberated.

The Buddha told Subhuti: Good men and good women who have aroused the great mind of becoming a Buddha and liberating beings should thus give rise to the mind: I should liberate all beings and bring them to Buddhahood, and yet when all beings have thus been liberated and brought to Buddhahood, in truth there is no such affair as beings being liberated and attaining Buddhahood.

Cultivation is the cultivation of the mind, which is to say, how one should give rise to the mind. The essence of the two questions “How should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?” is: how should a cultivator give rise to the mind? Therefore the World-Honored One here uses “should thus give rise to the mind” to answer both questions at once: to vow to liberate all beings while not dwelling in dharmas—that is, even if one liberates all beings and brings them to Buddhahood, one does not cling to the mark of a self, the mark of a human, the mark of a being, or the mark of a life, nor to the mark of dharmas, nor to the mark of non-dharmas.

Thus should one abide and uphold it; thus should one subdue one's mind: even if one liberates all beings and brings them to Buddhahood, one does not cling to marks in the slightest (“and not one being has in fact been liberated”), how much less in other matters.
This passage of teaching has several layers of meaning:

First, since one is to liberate all beings and bring them to Buddhahood, one will no longer stand opposed to beings. One will not harm them, will not envy them, will not despise them, will not contend with them for fame and profit. When beings intrude upon one, or even harm one, one will not give rise to anger. In liberating all beings, this stubborn “I” dissolves, and afflictions are naturally subdued.

Second, to liberate all beings and bring them to Buddhahood is by no means a matter of one lifetime (to the end of this present life); as long as there remains a single moment within the dream of ignorance, one must do one's utmost, and so one naturally abides and upholds it.

Third, to liberate all beings and bring them to Buddhahood is an affair within the dream of ignorance, and of course not one being has in fact been liberated. Yet to be able to give rise to such a mind depends on one's skill in detachment from marks. If one's skill in detachment from marks has reached the point that “when all beings have been liberated, not one being has in fact been liberated,” what need one fear that the work of the Way will not be accomplished? As the saying goes: since one is already in Hanyuan Hall, why ask where Chang'an is.

[Since one is already in Hanyuan Hall, why ask where Chang'an is] Hanyuan Hall was the name of a palace of the Tang dynasty, famous because of the “Rhapsody on Hanyuan Hall” written by Li Hua of the Tang. Chang'an was the capital of the Tang; to be in Hanyuan Hall is naturally to be within the capital.

Why? Subhuti! If a bodhisattva has the mark of a self, the mark of a human, the mark of a being, or the mark of a life, he is not a bodhisattva. Why is this? Subhuti! In truth there is no dharma by which one arouses the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Subhuti! If a bodhisattva falsely clings to all dharmas as truly existent (having the mark of a self, the mark of a human, the mark of a being, the mark of a life), he is not a bodhisattva. (This sentence repeats the teaching of the third section.) Why is this said? Because even the very matter of arousing the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is itself illusion. (The “dharma” of “in truth there is no dharma” here means the dharma of things and phenomena.)
Question: Why is it said that the very matter of arousing the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is itself illusion?

Answer: Because the “I” that arouses the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is illusion, and anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is also illusion (see the seventh section: “There is no fixed dharma called anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”).

The question Subhuti raised was: “Good men and good women who arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—how should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?” The World-Honored One answered in the passage above. Going further, the very matter of arousing the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is itself illusion.

Subhuti! What do you think? At the place of Dipankara Buddha, did the Tathāgata obtain any dharma of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? No, World-Honored One! As I understand the meaning the Buddha has spoken, at the place of Dipankara Buddha the Buddha had no dharma by which to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

The World-Honored One asked: Subhuti! What do you think, was there at the place of Dipankara Buddha such a thing as the Tathāgata attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? Subhuti answered: No, World-Honored One! As I understand the meaning the Buddha has spoken, at the place of Dipankara Buddha the Buddha had no such thing as attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Here it is taught that the matter of becoming a Buddha is not existent but is illusion. Because Subhuti himself had not yet had the experience of “attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,” he answered on the basis of the Buddha's teaching.

[At the place of Dipankara Buddha the Buddha had no dharma by which to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi] The Buddha, on the causal ground, though ascending to the Buddha-way, in truth accomplished nothing: it was accomplishing by accomplishing nothing.

Compare “Chapter Ten, on Adorning the Pure Land”: “The Buddha told Subhuti: What do you think? In former days, at the place of Dipankara Buddha, did the Tathāgata obtain any dharma? No, World-Honored One! At the place of Dipankara Buddha the Tathāgata in truth obtained no dharma.”

The Tathāgata liberates beings, yet in truth none are liberated; though in truth none are liberated, it is liberating by liberating none. The Tathāgata becomes a Buddha, yet in truth nothing is accomplished; though in truth nothing is accomplished, it is accomplishing by accomplishing nothing.

The two passages above say: one does not see (does not form the thought) that there are beings to be liberated, nor does one see (does not form the thought) that there is a Buddha to be accomplished, because liberating beings and becoming a Buddha are both affairs within the dream of ignorance: using illusion to transcend illusion, one must not cling to them as real.

The Buddha said: So it is, so it is. Subhuti! In truth there is no dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhuti! If there were a dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Dipankara Buddha would not have given me the prophecy: In a future life you shall become a Buddha, with the name Shakyamuni. But because in truth there is no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Dipankara Buddha gave me the prophecy, saying: In a future life you shall become a Buddha, with the name Shakyamuni.
The Buddha said: So it is, so it is.”
—The World-Honored One greatly affirmed and praised Subhuti's answer.

Subhuti! In truth there is no dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhuti! If there were a dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Dipankara Buddha would not have given me the prophecy: In a future life you shall become a Buddha, with the name Shakyamuni.”

—Subhuti! In truth there is no such thing as “the Tathāgata attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.” Subhuti! If there were a dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Dipankara Buddha would not have given me the prophecy: In a future life you shall become a Buddha, with the name Shakyamuni.

[If there were a dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Dipankara Buddha would not have given me the prophecy] The Tathāgata's attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is not truly existent, and so I should not form the thought: I have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. If I formed the thought that I have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I would still be clinging to the mark of “attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi”; that is practicing a conditioned dharma, and one has already strayed from the Buddha-way. Dipankara Buddha would of course not have given me the prophecy: In a future life you shall become a Buddha.

Because in truth there is no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Dipankara Buddha gave me the prophecy, saying: In a future life you shall become a Buddha, with the name Shakyamuni.”

—Because the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is illusion, and I also do not form the thought that there is truly a dharma by which the Tathāgata attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, therefore Dipankara Buddha gave me the prophecy.
Why? The Tathāgata means the meaning that all dharmas are thus.
Why is this said? Because “Tathāgata” means realizing that all dharmas are originally thus (originally as they are).

If someone says that the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhuti! In truth there is no dharma by which the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhuti! The anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi the Tathāgata attained is therein neither real nor empty.

If someone says that the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—Subhuti! I tell you in truth, there truly is no such thing as “the Buddha attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.” The matter of the Tathāgata's becoming a Buddha is neither existent nor non-existent; it is illusion.

[Neither real nor empty] Neither existent nor non-existent. [The anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi the Tathāgata attained is therein neither real nor empty] The matter of becoming a Buddha is neither existent nor non-existent; it is illusion.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddhadharma.
Therefore, all dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata are the dharma of the Way of becoming a Buddha.

[Therefore] The tone carries on from the passage above: “the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi the Tathāgata attained is therein neither real nor empty.” [The Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddhadharma] Though the Tathāgata's becoming a Buddha is illusion, yet within the dream of ignorance the Tathāgata truly became a Buddha, and so the dharmas the Tathāgata speaks within the dream of ignorance are all the dharma of the Way of becoming a Buddha.

Concerning the scriptural sentence “Therefore the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddhadharma,” there have traditionally been two explanations. From the context, “Buddhadharma” here means the dharma of becoming a Buddha; on this point there is no dispute. But as to the meaning of this sentence, because of different punctuation there are two views:
First: “Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddhadharma.” (Meaning: therefore, all dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata are the dharma of becoming a Buddha.)
Second: “Therefore, the Tathāgata says: all dharmas are Buddhadharma.” (Meaning: therefore, the Tathāgata says: all dharmas are the dharma of becoming a Buddha.)

Those who hold the first view include the Great Compendium of a Hundred Commentaries on the Diamond Sutra, where, under the scriptural sentence “Therefore the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddhadharma,” Wang Rixiu comments: “For this reason, the Buddha says that all dharmas are to be used in cultivation and are the dharma of becoming a Buddha.”
Wang Rixiu

That is, the layman Longshu of the Song dynasty, who wrote the Discourse on the Pure Land and edited the Great Amitābha Sutra. When the layman was about to leave the world, he took leave of all his relatives and friends, and urged them on in the work of the Pure Land. Before his death he still lectured and recited with his disciples and bowed to the Buddha as usual, and at death he passed away standing upright.

This book adopts the first view, for the reason that, judging from the essential purport and thread of the sutra's meaning, it should read “Therefore, all dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata are the dharma of becoming a Buddha.” Secondly, “Buddhadharma” here means the dharma of becoming a Buddha. If it were interpreted as “Therefore, the Tathāgata says: all dharmas are the dharma of becoming a Buddha,” then the heretical teachings, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying, and so on, would also be the dharma of becoming a Buddha—and this assertion (that all dharmas are the dharma of becoming a Buddha) especially risks being abused. Must one not be careful? If, out of greed for worldly pleasures, one makes the excuse “eating without eating” or “doing without doing,” that is extremely dangerous. The Song of Certifying the Way says: “Clever emptiness, denying cause and effect, vast and boundless, invites calamity and disaster; abandoning existence and clinging to emptiness is the same disease, like fleeing drowning and throwing oneself into fire.”

Yet, on the other hand, the assertion that “all dharmas are the dharma of becoming a Buddha” is correct when spoken at a deeper level. As the Essentials of the Transmission of the Mind says: “All form is Buddha-form, all sound is Buddha-sound.” But one may speak thus only when one has awakened to the corresponding ground. Just as, generally speaking, pouring water will put out a fire, yet if the fire is a blazing inferno, the water poured on is broken down by the high temperature into hydrogen and oxygen: hydrogen can burn of itself and oxygen supports combustion, and the fire blazes the more fiercely. One who has reached this ground finds that “the yellow flowers beyond the window are none of them other than prajñā; the green bamboos before the courtyard are all true suchness.” If one examines it thus, then every matter can be tempered, every moment is practice, everywhere there is benefit, and every place is Buddhadharma.
Subhuti! What is spoken of as all dharmas is not all dharmas; therefore it is called all dharmas.

Subhuti! What is spoken of as all dharmas (having marks) is not all dharmas (no substance); therefore it is called all dharmas (is illusion). This says that all dharmas have marks, have no substance, and are illusion.

Considering that beings might again cling to the Buddhadharma, the World-Honored One added with care: the Buddha says all dharmas are illusion. Since the beginningless kalpa, beings have either clung to existence or clung to nothingness—a habit formed over life after life, extremely stubborn; and so the World-Honored One says again and again in this sutra: not existent, not non-existent, but illusion.
Compare the eighth section: “Subhuti! What is called Buddhadharma is not Buddhadharma; therefore it is called Buddhadharma.”

Subhuti! For example, a human body is tall and great. Subhuti said: World-Honored One! The Tathāgata says a human body is tall and great, which is not a great body; therefore it is called a great body.

Subhuti! For example, a human body is tall and great. Subhuti said: World-Honored One! The Tathāgata says a human body is tall and great (having marks), which is not a great body (no substance); therefore it is called a great body (is illusion).

In the tenth section there is this passage: “Subhuti! Suppose there were a person whose body were like the king of Mount Sumeru: what do you think, is that body great? Subhuti said: Very great, World-Honored One! Why? The Buddha says it is no body; therefore it is called a great body.” There the World-Honored One had taught the rule of the pure mind (“they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere”), and then tossed out this topic of the supreme wondrous reward-body, of such interest to cultivators, to see how well Subhuti had grasped and mastered this rule of the pure mind. Subhuti's first sentence, “Very great,” was like a mirror reflecting an object—this was right. In the second sentence he said at once that this body is illusion, closely guarding the original mind and not dragged by conditions. This shows that the Elder Subhuti has not only understood the rule of the pure mind but applies it well, setting us an example: thought after thought, abiding in the Way. Now the World-Honored One says again: “Subhuti! For example, a human body is tall and great.” So Subhuti says at once: “World-Honored One! The Tathāgata says a human body is tall and great, which is not a great body; therefore it is called a great body.” This is his example of closely guarding the original mind and not being dragged by conditions.

Subhuti! A bodhisattva is also thus. If he says, “I shall liberate immeasurable beings,” then he is not called a bodhisattva. Why? Subhuti! In truth there is no dharma called a bodhisattva. Therefore the Buddha says that all dharmas are without self, without human, without being, without life.

Subhuti! The great body is illusion, and the bodhisattva is also illusion. If a bodhisattva thinks, “I shall liberate immeasurable beings,” he is not a bodhisattva. Why? Subhuti! Truly speaking, there is no such thing as a bodhisattva. Therefore the Buddha says there is no such dharma as self, human, being, or life.

[If he says, “I shall liberate immeasurable beings,” then he is not called a bodhisattva] A bodhisattva liberating beings must not cling to marks. “If he says, ‘I shall liberate immeasurable beings’”—this is clinging to marks. Cultivation is meant to turn delusion into awakening, and clinging to marks is delusion; so cultivation that clings to marks cannot succeed—it is what is called boiling sand and expecting rice. Therefore one who practices the six perfections while clinging to marks is not called a bodhisattva. A bodhisattva should say: I shall liberate immeasurable beings, and yet in truth not one being is liberated. [In truth there is no dharma called a bodhisattva] There truly is no such thing as “called a bodhisattva.” This says that a bodhisattva is illusion and not truly existent, echoing the passage above, “in truth there is no dharma by which the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.” [The Buddha says that all dharmas are without self, without human, without being, without life] This says that there simply is no such thing as self, human, being, or life; they are all illusion.

Subhuti! If a bodhisattva says, “I shall adorn the Buddha-land,” he is not called a bodhisattva. Why? The Tathāgata says that what is called the adornment of Buddha-lands is not adornment; therefore it is called adornment. Subhuti! If a bodhisattva comprehends the dharma of no-self, the Tathāgata names him a true bodhisattva.

Subhuti! If a bodhisattva thinks, “I shall adorn the Buddha-land,” he is not called a bodhisattva. Why is this said? Because adorning the Buddha-land is illusion, and to take illusion as real (“I shall adorn the Buddha-land”) is therefore not a bodhisattva. Subhuti! If a bodhisattva comprehends the dharma of no-self (no self of persons, no self of dharmas), such a bodhisattva the Tathāgata names a true bodhisattva. (See “Chapter Ten, on Adorning the Pure Land”: “Subhuti! What do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn the Buddha-land? No, World-Honored One! Why? What is called the adornment of Buddha-lands is not adornment; therefore it is called adornment.”)

Since there is no such thing as self, human, being, or life, a bodhisattva cultivating the six perfections and ten thousand practices to adorn the Buddha-land must likewise not cling to marks. Only one who comprehends the dharma of no-self is truly a bodhisattva.

Above it was said that body and mind are illusion; now it is said that becoming a Buddha is illusion, that self, human, being, and life are illusion, and that a bodhisattva's cultivation adorning the Buddha-land is also illusion. Then who is cultivating? And how does one cultivate?
In the Complete Enlightenment Sutra, Bodhisattva Samantabhadra raised this very question:

“World-Honored One, if those beings know that all is like illusion, and body and mind are also illusion, how can one use illusion to cultivate further illusion? If the nature of all illusions is utterly extinguished, then there is no mind—who is it that cultivates? And why does he again speak of cultivating as illusion? If beings do not cultivate at all, and within birth and death forever dwell in illusion, never knowing the realm of illusion, how can their deluded minds be liberated? May you, for the sake of all beings in the last age, provide the skillful means by which they may practice step by step, so that all beings may forever leave all illusions.”
The World-Honored One taught in reply:

“Good man! All the various illusions of all beings are born from the Tathāgata's perfect enlightenment wondrous mind, just as sky-flowers arise from the sky: though the illusory flowers vanish, the nature of the sky is not destroyed. The illusory mind of beings is in turn extinguished in reliance on illusion; when all illusions are utterly extinguished, the enlightened mind does not move. To speak of enlightenment in reliance on illusion is also called illusion; if one says there is enlightenment, one has not yet left illusion; and to say there is no enlightenment is likewise so. Therefore the extinction of illusion is named the unmoving.”
